Clinical Reference

Alcohol Withdrawal

On this page
A hyperexcitable, hyperadrenergic rebound state that emerges hours after a chronic heavy drinker cuts down or stops — the brain, having silenced its own inhibition to counter alcohol, is suddenly left with the brakes off and the accelerator floored.
Spectrum: tremor → hallucinosis → seizures → delirium tremens Treat when CIWA-Ar ≥ 8–10 Untreated DTs mortality up to ~15–40% Anchor Rx: symptom-triggered benzodiazepines Predict risk with PAWSS ≥ 4
Shared

Pathophysiology

🧬

Mechanism — the story

Ethanol is a global CNS depressant with two dominant molecular actions: it is a positive allosteric potentiator of the inhibitory GABA-A receptor (it makes the brain's main "off switch" more effective) and an antagonist of the excitatory NMDA glutamate receptor (it dampens the brain's main "on switch"). With chronic heavy exposure the brain fights to restore its normal set-point: it down-regulates GABA-A receptors (fewer, less-sensitive inhibitory channels) and up-regulates NMDA/glutamate receptors (more excitatory machinery). The drinker now needs alcohol just to feel normal — a new, alcohol-dependent equilibrium.

When alcohol is abruptly removed, both adaptations are suddenly unopposed: inhibition is blunted while excitation is amplified. The result is a runaway glutamatergic storm plus a surge of noradrenergic (locus coeruleus) output — clinically, tremor, autonomic hyperactivity, seizures, and delirium. Layered on top, dopaminergic dysregulation drives hallucinations. This is the causal chain the whole guide hangs on: every effective drug either replaces the lost GABA inhibition or damps the excess glutamate/adrenergic drive. (StatPearls NBK441882; PMC4606320)

Alcohol is a brake pedal held down for years. The brain adapts by wearing down the brake pads (GABA-A) and installing a bigger engine (NMDA). As long as the foot stays on the brake, the car cruises. Stop drinking, and you lift the foot off worn brakes attached to an over-sized engine — the car lurches forward out of control. Benzodiazepines and phenobarbital are a spare set of brake pads; you re-install them, then taper them off slowly as the brain rebuilds its own.
The two chronic adaptations (GABA-A down, NMDA up) become dangerous only when alcohol is removed. Theme-adaptive SVG — lightens in light mode.
Ethanol (C₂H₅OH) — the small, freely CNS-penetrant molecule behind both GABA-A potentiation and NMDA inhibition.
Wikimedia Commons · Bryan Derksen · Public domain — source
A ligand-gated ion channel — the receptor family to which GABA-A (Cl⁻ influx → inhibition) and NMDA (Ca²⁺/Na⁺ influx → excitation) belong. Alcohol tunes both.
Wikimedia Commons · Bensaccount · Public domain — source
Benzodiazepines & phenobarbital restore GABA-A inhibition (re-install the brakes) — first-line. Phenobarbital additionally blocks glutamate/AMPA and prolongs channel opening independent of endogenous GABA, so it still works when benzodiazepine receptors are saturated. Dexmedetomidine & clonidine (central α2-agonists) blunt the noradrenergic surge but do nothing for the seizure risk. Propofol & ketamine hit the NMDA arm directly for refractory cases. Gabapentin/carbamazepine stabilize neuronal excitability for milder disease. Keep this map in mind through every ladder below.
⏱️

Timeline — what appears when

Symptoms unfold in a predictable (if overlapping) sequence timed from the last drink. Hour-windows are classic teaching; StatPearls gives broader, overlapping ranges (seizures 8–48 h; DTs 3–8 days). Knowing the clock tells you what to expect next and when the patient is still climbing toward peak danger.

The rising staircase of alcohol withdrawal. A patient who seizes at 24 h can still progress to DTs at 72 h — do not relax monitoring after a seizure resolves.
🗂️

Definitions & classification

DSM-5 alcohol withdrawal — ≥ 2 of 8 after cutting down heavy/prolonged use

Autonomic hyperactivity (sweats, HR >100) · hand tremor · insomnia · nausea/vomiting · transient visual/tactile/auditory hallucinations or illusions · psychomotor agitation · anxiety · generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Must cause distress/impairment and not be better explained otherwise. (DSM-5; StatPearls NBK441882)

SyndromeOnset from last drinkHallmarkSensorium
Minor / uncomplicated6–12 h (peaks ~24–72 h)Tremor, anxiety, N/V, sweating, insomnia, mild HTN/tachycardiaNormal
Alcoholic hallucinosis12–24 h (resolves ~48 h)Visual > auditory/tactile hallucinations with normal vitalsIntact & oriented
Withdrawal seizures ("rum fits")24–48 h (StatPearls 8–48 h; peak ~24 h)Generalized tonic-clonic, single or brief flurry; ~3–5% of withdrawalsPost-ictal only
Delirium tremens (DTs)48–96 h (StatPearls 3–8 d)Global confusion, agitation, fever, severe autonomic instabilityClouded / delirious
Hallucinosis vs DTs is a classic board and bedside distinction: hallucinosis has a clear sensorium and normal vitals; DTs has delirium plus autonomic storm. Only DTs carries the high mortality — treated ~1–4%, untreated historically ~15–40%. (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delirium_tremens; StatPearls)

Assess

Presentation & who is at risk

🔍

Signs & symptoms — frequency and why they happen

Withdrawal should be suspected in any heavy drinker who reduces intake — planned quit, running out of money, or an intercurrent admission that interrupts drinking. Ask about the last drink, typical daily quantity, and prior withdrawal history (the single best predictor of future severity).

Feature~FrequencyWhy it happens (mechanism)
Tremor (fine, postural)~75%Loss of GABAergic inhibition + noradrenergic surge → increased motor-neuron firing and muscle-spindle sensitivity
Anxiety / irritability~75%Unopposed limbic glutamatergic excitation and locus-coeruleus noradrenergic output
Autonomic: tachycardia, hypertension, diaphoresis~70%Adrenergic overactivity from loss of the alcohol "brake" on the sympathetic nervous system
Insomnia / vivid dreams~55%REM rebound and cortical hyperexcitability once alcohol's sleep-suppressing GABA effect is withdrawn
Nausea / vomiting / anorexia~50%Autonomic dysregulation plus direct gastric irritation and delayed gastric emptying
Headache~45%Cerebral vasomotor changes and adrenergic drive (a CIWA-Ar item)
Hallucinations (visual > tactile/auditory)~25%Dopaminergic dysregulation + sensory-cortex hyperexcitability; classically with intact sensorium (hallucinosis)
Withdrawal seizure (GTC)~3–5%Glutamate/NMDA up-regulation lowers seizure threshold; kindling raises risk with each prior withdrawal
Delirium tremens~3–5%Extreme, sustained excitatory/adrenergic storm with global cerebral dysfunction
Kindling: each completed withdrawal episode makes the next one worse and lowers the seizure/DT threshold. A history of prior withdrawal, seizures, or DTs is the strongest reason to treat aggressively and monitor closely — it is a core PAWSS item below.
Score

PAWSS — predict complicated withdrawal

Prediction of Alcohol Withdrawal Severity Scale (Maldonado). Use at intake to decide who needs inpatient monitoring/prophylaxis. Each item = 1 point (max 10). First confirm the threshold gate — if neither is true, PAWSS = 0 and the tool does not apply.

Workup

What to order & when

🧪

Labs — and how to read them

CBCMacrocytosis (↑MCV) is a chronic-alcohol clue; thrombocytopenia from marrow suppression / hypersplenism raises bleed risk.Initial
CMP + Mg + PhosCorrect hypoglycemia, hypomagnesemia (lowers seizure threshold, refractory to Rx until fixed), hypokalemia, hypophosphatemia (refeeding). Assess renal (drives gabapentin/acamprosate).Initial
LFTs, GGT, PT/INR, albuminAST:ALT > 2:1 and ↑GGT suggest alcoholic liver injury; INR/albumin gauge synthetic function → shifts benzo choice to lorazepam.Initial
LipaseScreen for alcoholic pancreatitis if abdominal pain/vomiting.If symptoms
Ethanol level + urine toxA positive level with active withdrawal signals severe tolerance; tox uncovers co-ingested benzodiazepines/opioids/stimulants.Initial
PEth / CDT / %CDTBiomarkers of sustained heavy use — useful to confirm relapse or monitor abstinence in clinic.Optional
Imaging (CT head / MRI)Not routine. CT head for first seizure, focal deficit, head trauma, or atypical/persistent delirium; MRI if Wernicke suspected (mammillary-body / periaqueductal FLAIR change).If indicated
LabDirectionWhy it moves · confounders
GGT↑Enzyme induction by alcohol; sensitive but non-specific (also ↑ with any hepatic enzyme induction, biliary disease). Falls with abstinence over weeks.
AST : ALT ratio> 2:1Alcohol depletes pyridoxal-5′-phosphate needed for ALT synthesis; mitochondrial AST released. Very high transaminases (>500) argue against pure alcoholic hepatitis.
MCV↑Direct marrow toxicity + folate deficiency; lags and normalizes slowly (RBC lifespan ~120 d).
Magnesium↓Poor intake, GI losses, renal wasting. Must be repleted — hypomagnesemia sustains seizures and blunts response to therapy.
Phosphate↓Chronic depletion; drops further with refeeding/dextrose. Severe hypophosphatemia → respiratory-muscle weakness.
Platelets↓Marrow suppression, hypersplenism, folate deficiency; recover over days of abstinence.
Treat

Outpatient management

💊

Who is eligible, then first-line → escalation

Outpatient detox is appropriate only for mild, low-risk withdrawal: PAWSS <4, CIWA-Ar <10, no history of seizures or DTs, no serious comorbidity (advanced liver disease, CAD, pregnancy), no uncontrolled co-substance use, and a reliable support person plus daily follow-up. Anyone failing these → treat inpatient.
1
Benzodiazepine taper — the outpatient anchor
Long-acting, self-tapering agents; fixed-schedule taper over 3–5 days.
▾
A benzodiazepine re-supplies GABA-A inhibition (the worn brake pads) and is then tapered so the brain re-grows its own inhibition without a rebound.
DrugStartTaper (titration)Why / notesIf liver disease / elderly
Chlordiazepoxide50 mg PO QID day 1→ 50 mg TID → 25 mg TID → 25 mg BID → stop (~by day 4–5)Long half-life gives a smooth self-taper; classic outpatient choiceSwitch to lorazepam/oxazepam (no active metabolites)
Diazepam10 mg PO QID day 1→ 10 mg TID → 5 mg TID → 5 mg BID → stopVery long-acting; active metabolite (desmethyldiazepam) prolongs auto-taperAvoid — accumulates in cirrhosis; use lorazepam
Lorazepam2 mg PO TID day 1→ 1 mg TID → 1 mg BID → 0.5 mg BID → stopGlucuronidated (non-oxidative) — preferred when liver function is impaired or age >65This is the alternative; oxazepam 15–30 mg is equivalent

Dispense small quantities with daily/every-other-day pickup or a supervising family member. Counsel: no driving, no additional alcohol, no other sedatives. (ASAM 2020; PMC4606320)

2
Benzodiazepine-sparing alternatives — gabapentin / carbamazepine
For mild–moderate disease, or when benzodiazepines are undesirable.
▾
DrugStartTitration → targetWhy it worksCautions / alt
Gabapentin900 mg/day divided (300 mg TID) or 300 mg TID900 mg TID ×4 d → 600 mg TID ×3 d → 300 mg TID ×2 d → stop (RCT up to 1200 mg/day)Modulates neuronal excitability; reduces craving and eases sleep/anxiety — bonus for co-existing AUDRenally cleared — reduce if eGFR <60; misuse potential
Carbamazepine200 mg PO TID–QID day 1Taper over 5 days to 200 mg/day → stopAnticonvulsant that stabilizes membranes; ASAM-endorsed mild–moderate alternativeHyponatremia, marrow suppression, CYP inducer; avoid in cytopenias
Gabapentin and carbamazepine do not prevent seizures or DTs as reliably as benzodiazepines — reserve them for genuinely mild, low-risk patients (ASAM 2020: benzodiazepines remain first-line for moderate–severe).
3
Relapse prevention — treat the underlying AUD
Start once the acute withdrawal is settled; this is where mortality benefit lives.
▾
DrugStart → TargetWhy it worksContraindication / alt
Naltrexone (PO)50 mg PO daily (may start 25 mg ×3 d)µ-opioid antagonist — blunts alcohol's rewarding dopamine surge; first-line (APA 2018), reduces heavy-drinking days (COMBINE)Avoid in acute hepatitis/liver failure or current opioid use → use acamprosate
Naltrexone XR (IM)380 mg IM every 4 weeksSame mechanism; guarantees adherence for patients who miss pillsSame opioid caveat; needs gluteal injection
Acamprosate666 mg (2×333 mg) PO TIDModulates glutamate/GABA back toward balance in abstinence; first-line, liver-safeAvoid if severe renal impairment (CrCl <30); TID pill burden
Disulfiram250 mg PO dailyBlocks aldehyde dehydrogenase → toxic acetaldehyde reaction deters drinking (aversive)Only for motivated, supervised, abstinent patients; avoid CAD, hepatic disease
Topiramate / gabapentinTopiramate titrate to ~150–300 mg/day; gabapentin up to ~1200 mg/daySecond-line (APA 2018) when first-line not tolerated/effectiveTopiramate: cognitive slowing, acidosis, stones

COMBINE (JAMA 2006, n=1,383): naltrexone conferred benefit under medical management; acamprosate showed no significant effect and the combination was not superior — but acamprosate remains valuable when naltrexone is contraindicated. Refer to addiction services/behavioral counseling in parallel.

Monitor

Follow-up cadence

📈

What to recheck, and when

  • Daily contact days 1–3 (in person or phone) during an outpatient taper — the window of peak seizure/DT risk. Escalate to ED for worsening tremor, hallucinations, confusion, fever, or a missed dose with rebound.
  • Vitals & brief CIWA-style check at each visit; hold/advance the taper by response.
  • LFTs, GGT, CBC, PEth/CDT at 2–4 weeks and periodically to track abstinence and hepatic recovery.
  • Renal function before/while on acamprosate; LFTs before oral naltrexone and periodically.
  • Continue thiamine 100 mg PO daily (plus folate/multivitamin) through the outpatient course.
Prevent

USPSTF A/B & screening

🛡️

Grade A & B recommendations relevant to alcohol

GradeRecommendationPopulation / how
BScreen for unhealthy alcohol use & provide brief behavioral counseling (USPSTF 2018)All adults ≥18 incl. pregnant persons; use AUDIT-C or the NIAAA single question ("How many times in the past year 5 [men]/4 [women]+ drinks in a day?")
BScreen for depression in adultsOverlaps heavily with AUD; treat both
BHepatitis C screening in adults 18–79Higher prevalence in heavy drinkers with liver disease

NIAAA low-risk limits: men ≤4 drinks/day and ≤14/week; women ≤3/day and ≤7/week. One standard drink = 14 g ethanol. Vaccinate (hepatitis A/B, pneumococcal, influenza) given liver and aspiration risk. (USPSTF 2018; NIAAA)

Escalate

When to refer / admit

🚑

Red flags → ED / admission

Send to the ED — do not manage in clinic — for any of: PAWSS ≥4 or CIWA-Ar ≥15; history of withdrawal seizures or DTs; a seizure now; hallucinations or confusion; temperature >38.3 °C; HR >120 or SBP >180 despite a benzodiazepine dose; pregnancy; serious comorbidity (decompensated cirrhosis, CAD, pancreatitis, GI bleed); inability to tolerate oral intake; or no reliable support/follow-up.
🛏️ Wards — acute inpatient management
Admit

Who to admit

📋

Admission criteria & risk profile

Admit to a monitored floor bed when withdrawal is moderate–severe or the patient carries high-risk features:

  • PAWSS ≥4 or CIWA-Ar ≥15, or escalating scores despite oral therapy.
  • History of withdrawal seizures or DTs (kindling → high risk of complicated course).
  • A withdrawal seizure during this episode; hallucinations or any clouding of sensorium.
  • Significant comorbidity: decompensated liver disease, CAD/arrhythmia, pancreatitis, GI bleed, infection, poorly controlled diabetes, pregnancy.
  • Marked electrolyte derangement (Mg, K, Phos), dehydration, or inability to take oral medication.
  • Unsafe outpatient setting (no support, co-substance use).
The prior-withdrawal history predicts this admission better than the current vitals do — a calm-looking patient with a DT history can decompensate at 48–72 h. Anticipate, don't react.
Score

CIWA-Ar — monitor severity

Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment, revised (Sullivan 1989). Ten items; nine scored 0–7, orientation 0–4 → max 67. Drives symptom-triggered dosing. Valid only in a communicative patient — not in intubated/sedated/delirious ICU patients.

0
Minimal — no medication needed
Thresholds (StatPearls): ≤8 minimal · 8–15 moderate · >15 severe. Treat (give a benzodiazepine) for CIWA-Ar ≥8–10. Scale form · StatPearls

Acute management

💊

Benzodiazepine strategy → adjuncts → phenobarbital

Diazepam — a long-acting benzodiazepine whose active metabolites give a built-in self-taper.
Wikimedia Commons · Ben Mills · Public domain — source
ASAM 2020 favors symptom-triggered dosing (dose to the CIWA-Ar) over fixed schedules — it shortens length of stay and cuts total benzodiazepine exposure (Saitz 1994: 100 vs 425 mg chlordiazepoxide, 9 vs 68 h; Daeppen 2002: 37.5 vs 231 mg oxazepam) without more seizures or DTs.
1
Benzodiazepines — first-line
Symptom-triggered (CIWA ≥8–10); front-load for severe disease.
▾
DrugStart (symptom-triggered)Titration / front-loadWhy / when to pickIf liver disease / elderly
Diazepam10–20 mg PO/IV for CIWA ≥8–10Front-load: 10–20 mg IV q1–2h (or q5–10 min IV titration in severe) until light sedation; long half-life then self-tapersPreferred long-acting agent for smooth, self-tapering controlAccumulates in cirrhosis → switch to lorazepam
Chlordiazepoxide50–100 mg PO for CIWA ≥8–10Repeat q1–2h PRN by score; taper as scores fallLong-acting oral option for cooperative floor patientsAvoid in significant liver disease
Lorazepam2–4 mg PO/IV/IM for CIWA ≥8–10Repeat q1h PRN; front-load 2–4 mg IV q15–20 min in severeGlucuronidated, no active metabolites — the choice in liver failure, the elderly, or when IV/IM neededThis is the alternative; oxazepam 15–30 mg PO equivalent

Equivalence: 5 mg diazepam ≈ 25 mg chlordiazepoxide ≈ 1 mg lorazepam ≈ 15 mg oxazepam. Monitor for over-sedation/respiratory depression, especially with co-ingested opioids. (ASAM 2020; PMC4606320; UCSF Hospital Handbook)

2
Adjuncts — gabapentin / carbamazepine / clonidine
Layer on for milder disease or persistent autonomic/anxiety symptoms.
▾
DrugStart → targetWhy it worksCautions
Gabapentin300–600 mg TID; taper over daysReduces excitability, anxiety, insomnia; benzodiazepine-sparingRenal dosing; sedation with benzos
Carbamazepine200 mg TID–QID → taper over ~5 dMembrane-stabilizing anticonvulsant for mild–moderateHyponatremia, marrow suppression
Clonidine0.1 mg PO BID–TIDCentral α2-agonist blunts adrenergic surge (HR/BP, tremor)Masks tachycardia that CIWA relies on; does not prevent seizures — adjunct only
Haloperidol0.5–2 mg for agitation/hallucinations onlyDopamine blockade for refractory agitation after adequate benzodiazepinesLowers seizure threshold, prolongs QT — never a substitute for benzodiazepines; use sparingly
3
Phenobarbital — for high benzodiazepine requirement
Add when benzodiazepines alone aren't controlling the patient.
▾
Phenobarbital potentiates GABA-A (prolongs channel open time) and antagonizes glutamate/AMPA — hitting both arms of the pathophysiology. Because it doesn't need endogenous GABA, it works when benzodiazepine receptors are saturated. Its long half-life (~53–118 h) builds in a self-taper.
RegimenDoseEvidence
ED single load (adjunct)10 mg/kg IV in 100 mL NS once, on top of a benzodiazepine protocolRosenson 2013 RCT: ICU admission 8% vs 25% (placebo), no added adverse events
Ward fixed-dose (no active DT)~64.8–97.2 mg PO TID ×48 h, then extended taperTidwell 2018: shorter ICU/hospital LOS vs CIWA/benzodiazepine standard
Active DTIV phenobarbital 260 mg (then per protocol)Tidwell 2018 protocol arm
Watch the combined sedation of benzodiazepine + phenobarbital — monitor respiratory rate and mental status; escalate to a higher level of care if you're stacking large doses.
Interactions

Comorbidities & drugs to avoid

🔗

How comorbidity changes the plan

ComorbidityEffect on courseEffect on management
Cirrhosis / hepatic impairmentImpaired drug clearance → benzodiazepine accumulation, over-sedation, precipitated encephalopathyUse lorazepam or oxazepam (glucuronidated); avoid diazepam/chlordiazepoxide; watch for hepatic encephalopathy mimicking DTs
Wernicke–KorsakoffThiamine deficiency → ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, confusion; irreversible if missedHigh-dose IV thiamine before glucose; do not rely on 100 mg/day
HypomagnesemiaSustains seizures; blunts response to benzodiazepinesReplete Mg early and repeatedly; recheck
Concurrent benzodiazepine / opioid useAdditive respiratory depression; higher tolerance shifts dose needsTitrate carefully with monitoring; naloxone available; consider phenobarbital protocol
PregnancyWithdrawal risks mother and fetus; DTs dangerousTreat withdrawal (benzodiazepines) — untreated withdrawal is more harmful; involve OB; avoid disulfiram/topiramate
ElderlyProlonged sedation, delirium, fallsPrefer lorazepam; lower doses, frequent reassessment
Cardiac (CAD, AF / "holiday heart")Adrenergic surge → ischemia, arrhythmiaTelemetry; control withdrawal to reduce catecholamine load; rate control as needed
Alcoholic ketoacidosis / hypoglycemiaAnion-gap acidosis, low glucoseDextrose after thiamine, fluids, electrolytes
Use with caution / avoid: glucose before thiamine (precipitates Wernicke); haloperidol/antipsychotics as primary therapy (lower seizure threshold, prolong QT — adjunct for agitation only); long-acting benzodiazepines in advanced cirrhosis (accumulate → over-sedation/encephalopathy); β-blockers/clonidine as monotherapy (mask the autonomic signs CIWA depends on and don't prevent seizures); unmonitored opioids stacked on benzodiazepines.
Monitor

Daily management

📈

What to trend each day

  • CIWA-Ar trend and total 24-h benzodiazepine requirement (rising cumulative dose = escalating disease).
  • Vitals — HR, BP, temperature (fever suggests DTs or infection), respiratory rate/sedation level after dosing.
  • Mental status & orientation — emerging confusion signals progression toward DTs.
  • Electrolytes — Mg, K, Phos daily until stable; glucose.
  • Volume status and oral intake; resume nutrition (thiamine before carbs).
  • Begin AUD relapse-prevention planning and addiction referral before discharge.
Escalate

When to call ICU

⬆️

Floor → ICU triggers

Transfer to ICU for any of: delirium tremens; benzodiazepine-resistant withdrawal (needing >40 mg diazepam-equivalent/hour or escalating doses without control); need for continuous IV sedation (dexmedetomidine/propofol) or a phenobarbital load beyond floor capability; status epilepticus or repeated seizures; respiratory compromise / airway concern; hemodynamic instability (persistent HR >140, arrhythmia, SBP swings); temperature >40 °C; or inability to protect the airway.
Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness + where they go

Discharge readiness: CIWA-Ar consistently <8–10 off (or on minimal tapering) benzodiazepines for ~24 h; stable vitals and mental status; tolerating oral intake; electrolytes corrected; thiamine/nutrition addressed; AUD pharmacotherapy started and follow-up/counseling arranged; safe environment.

Home

Resolved withdrawal, reliable support, outpatient AUD plan + naltrexone/acamprosate started.

Home health

Home + nursing/therapy visits; useful with deconditioning or wound/liver care needs.

Residential rehab / SNF

Needs structured addiction treatment or skilled nursing; unsafe home environment.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Rarely — for functional recovery (e.g., alcoholic neuropathy/deconditioning) if ≥3 h therapy/day tolerated.

LTAC

Prolonged complex care (e.g., vent weaning) after severe ICU DTs course.

Palliative

End-stage liver disease with goals-of-care focus.
🫀 ICU — severe & refractory withdrawal / delirium tremens
Admit

ICU triggers

🚨

When it belongs in the unit

  • Delirium tremens — delirium + autonomic storm; historically up to ~15–40% mortality untreated, ~1–4% treated.
  • Benzodiazepine-resistant withdrawal — >40 mg diazepam-equivalent/hour or rapidly escalating cumulative doses without control (REBEL EM).
  • Need for continuous IV infusion (dexmedetomidine, propofol) or aggressive phenobarbital loading.
  • Status epilepticus or recurrent seizures.
  • Respiratory failure / airway compromise, severe hemodynamic instability, hyperthermia >40 °C, or significant concurrent illness (severe pancreatitis, GI bleed, sepsis).
CIWA-Ar is invalid once a patient is intubated, deeply sedated, or too delirious to answer — it requires a communicative patient. In the ICU, titrate to a sedation target (e.g., RASS) and clinical signs, not to a CIWA number.
Monitor

Monitoring & access

🩸

Lines, labs, targets

  • Continuous telemetry and frequent NIBP (or arterial line if on infusions / labile) for the autonomic storm.
  • Reliable IV access (often central) for high-dose/continuous sedatives and electrolyte drips.
  • Sedation scale (RASS) and delirium screen (CAM-ICU) in place of CIWA-Ar; titrate to a light, calm target.
  • Electrolytes (Mg, K, Phos, glucose) q6–12h; temperature (hyperthermia), CK if agitated/rigid (rhabdomyolysis), lactate.
  • High-dose IV thiamine continued; nutrition; VTE and skin care during prolonged agitation/restraint.
Support

Sedatives & adjunct infusions

💉

Which drip, the mechanism, and the dose

AgentMechanismDoseEffectWhen to pick
Diazepam / lorazepam (IV push, escalating)GABA-A positive allosteric modulatorDiazepam 10–20 mg IV q5–10 min; lorazepam 2–4 mg IV q15 min — titrate to light sedationRestores inhibition; controls seizures & agitationFirst-line for all; foundation before adjuncts
PhenobarbitalGABA-A (↑channel open time) + glutamate/AMPA antagonism; GABA-independentLoad 10 mg/kg IV (or 130–260 mg IV increments); long self-taperDeep, durable control even when benzos saturatedBenzodiazepine resistance / DTs — key escalation
DexmedetomidineCentral α2-agonist0.2–1.5 mcg/kg/hr infusion (usually no bolus)Controls autonomic surge & agitation; light sedation without respiratory depressionAdjunct for autonomic control — does NOT prevent seizures; never monotherapy
PropofolGABA-A agonist + NMDA antagonistTitrate infusion (e.g., 5–50 mcg/kg/min) — requires intubationDeep sedation; hits both pathophysiology armsIntubated, benzodiazepine-refractory DTs
KetamineNMDA receptor antagonistAdjunct infusion (per protocol)Reduces benzodiazepine need; less respiratory depressionAdjunct in refractory DTs to spare sedatives / avoid intubation
Escalation logic follows the mechanism: maximize GABAergic control first (benzodiazepine → phenobarbital), then layer dexmedetomidine for the adrenergic component and propofol/ketamine for the NMDA arm in intubated/refractory cases. Dexmedetomidine and clonidine control numbers but leave the seizure risk untreated — always keep a GABAergic backbone.
Airway

Airway & ventilation

🌬️

When to intubate; initial settings

Intubation in AWS is usually for airway protection / sedation needs, not primary lung failure: obtundation with aspiration risk, status epilepticus, escalating sedative requirements exceeding safe monitoring, or profound agitation refractory to therapy. Deep sedation with propofol becomes an option once the airway is secured.

Indication
Airway protection
obtundation, aspiration, refractory sedation
Mode
AC/VC
volume-control assist-control
Tidal volume
6–8 mL/kg IBW
lung-protective (lungs usually normal)
PEEP / FiO₂
5 / wean
SpO₂ 92–96%
Sedation
Propofol ± benzo
treat withdrawal, not just sedate
A tube does not treat withdrawal. Keep the GABAergic/phenobarbital backbone going even while intubated on propofol — otherwise the glutamatergic storm resurfaces the moment sedation lightens.
Rescue

Refractory delirium tremens

⚙️

The refractory algorithm

  1. Maximize benzodiazepines — aggressive front-loading/IV titration to light sedation.
  2. Add phenobarbital when requirement is high or resistance emerges (>40 mg diazepam-eq/hr) — mechanistically overcomes benzodiazepine resistance; consider a fixed-dose protocol given long half-life.
  3. Add dexmedetomidine for persistent autonomic hyperactivity/agitation (adjunct — not antiseizure).
  4. Intubate + propofol for refractory, dangerous agitation; add ketamine (NMDA antagonist) to spare sedatives.
  5. Relentless supportive care: correct magnesium/electrolytes, treat hyperthermia, hydrate, hunt for and treat occult infection or other delirium contributors.
DTs is a medical emergency — the autonomic storm can cause arrhythmia, hyperthermia, aspiration, and cardiovascular collapse. Under-treatment (fear of over-sedation) is the more common and more lethal error; titrate up until controlled.
Downgrade

When to downgrade

⬇️

De-escalation to the floor

Downgrade when: IV infusions weaned off (dexmedetomidine/propofol) with stable sedation; no seizures ≥24 h; delirium/autonomic instability resolving (HR <120, no fever, stable BP); transitioned to oral/scheduled benzodiazepine or a self-tapering phenobarbital course; airway secure/extubated; electrolytes stable and eating. Not yet if: still on any continuous sedative infusion, requiring frequent large IV benzodiazepine boluses, delirious with autonomic surges, or airway not yet safe.

Pearls

High-yield pearls

💡

Twelve things that change management

  1. Thiamine before glucose, always — a dextrose bolus in a thiamine-deplete brain can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy. High-dose IV, not 100 mg.
  2. Symptom-triggered beats fixed-dose (Saitz 1994, Daeppen 2002, ASAM 2020): less total benzodiazepine, shorter treatment — but only if the patient can be reliably assessed.
  3. CIWA-Ar is a monitoring tool, not a risk-prediction tool, and is invalid in intubated/sedated/non-verbal patients. Use PAWSS to predict at intake.
  4. Kindling is real — each prior withdrawal worsens the next. A DT/seizure history mandates aggressive treatment even if the patient looks calm now.
  5. Hallucinosis ≠ DTs — normal vitals and intact sensorium distinguish it; only DTs carries the high mortality.
  6. Liver disease → lorazepam/oxazepam (glucuronidated, no active metabolites); long-acting benzodiazepines accumulate and can precipitate encephalopathy.
  7. Phenobarbital works when benzodiazepines don't — it's GABA-independent and also blocks glutamate; a single 10 mg/kg ED load cut ICU admission from 25%→8% (Rosenson 2013).
  8. Dexmedetomidine and clonidine are adjuncts, never monotherapy — they mask autonomic signs and do not prevent seizures.
  9. Correct magnesium — hypomagnesemia sustains seizures and blunts the response to therapy.
  10. Haloperidol is a last-resort adjunct for agitation — it lowers the seizure threshold and prolongs QT; never a substitute for GABAergic control.
  11. Treat withdrawal in pregnancy — untreated withdrawal (and DTs) is more dangerous to mother and fetus than benzodiazepines.
  12. The admission is a window for AUD treatment — start naltrexone or acamprosate and arrange counseling; that's where the long-term mortality benefit lies (COMBINE 2006).
